as_told: The American bank robber Willie Sutton was asked why he robbed banks. He answered, "Because that's where the money is." The line is used as a rule for going straight to the obvious source of value, and in medicine as 'Sutton's law': test first for the most likely diagnosis.
lesson: Robbers, and anyone else seeking a payoff, go where the money is concentrated.
what_happened: The earliest telling I found is in the Saturday Evening Post of 20 January 1951, in an article by Robert M. Yoder; it says only that 'someone once asked' Sutton, and names no one. On 30 March 1952, after Sutton's arrest, the reporter Fred Curran wrote in The American Weekly that Sutton told him banks were 'where the money is' when explaining why he went back to banks from stealing jewels. In his 1976 book with Edward Linn, Sutton wrote that he never said it, that 'some enterprising reporter' made it up, and that he robbed banks because he enjoyed it. So the words are reported by a reporter and denied by Sutton, and no record settles which is right.

earliest_telling.where: "Someday They'll Get Slick Willie Sutton", The Saturday Evening Post, vol. 223, no. 30, page 17 (transcribed by Garson O'Toole in a post to the American Dialect Society list, 7 Feb 2013)

lesson_verdict.why: FBI figures for 2011 show loot taken in 4,534 of 5,086 robberies, burglaries and larcenies at U.S. federally insured banks, totalling about $38.3 million in cash, or about $8,500 per incident with loot, but they record nothing about why robbers chose banks. I found no study of how robbers choose targets by the amount of money held.

source.what: FBI, Bank Crime Statistics 2011 (annual report, 1 January to 31 December 2011)
source.quote: Loot was taken in 4,534 (89 percent) of the 5,086 incidents.

search_steps: Open Library full-text search '"that's where the money is" sutton' (3,256 hits; first 50 sorted by year): earliest was a 1979 Daily News picture book; 1993 'They Never Said It' and 1995 'Everything You Know Is Wrong' call the quote false.

Lead: web search results for Quote Investigator and Snopes (I did not read their pages in full) point to the 1951 Saturday Evening Post and to Sutton's 1976 denial. Saved and read Garson O'Toole's ADS-L post of 7 Feb 2013, which transcribes the 1951 Post (from Academic Search Premier), a 1952 Nevada State Journal item, the 15 Mar 1952 Redlands Daily Facts, the 30 Mar 1952 Curran interview (GenealogyBank) and the 1976 book.

Searched archive.org for Saturday Evening Post issues of January 1951: only the 27 January issue is there, not 20 January. Open Library exact-phrase search '"eye for the simple essential"' (a phrase from the 1951 article) returned no hits.

Found Sutton's 1976 book on archive.org (wheremoneywas00sutt, lending-only). Its search-inside endpoint refused the request (403); did not retry. Open Library full-text searches '"some enterprising reporter who apparently felt a need"' and '"bank robber's maxim" "never said it" "because I enjoyed it"' returned snippets from the book's own scan; saved both result files.
Found the 1953 book I, Willie Sutton (with Quentin Reynolds) on archive.org; did not check it.
Did not find the Curran interview or the Redlands item in free full text.
Lesson: saved the FBI Bank Crime Statistics 2011 annual report.
confidence_note: The 1951 and 1952 quotes come from a transcription in a mailing-list post by a quotation researcher, not from the magazines themselves, which I could not get. The 1976 quotes come from Open Library search snippets of the book's scan, not from a full text. Under the rules, Curran's report of what Sutton told him is a reporter's interview and counts as evidence only weakly; it conflicts with Sutton's own published denial, written 24 years later by a man who also says he might well have said it. I treated the conflict as unresolved, which gives 'unsupported'.
